rows.evidence: unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-12 evidence: New displayed result since 9b6be31, re-derived. Claim: with h = 1/alpha, h P0(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) + E0[sum_{k<=n} (M_k - h) 1_{A_k}] <= 1. Derivation: Theorem 6.4's proof gives E0[W_n] <= 1 with W_n = sum_k M_k 1_{A_k} + M_n 1_{B_n}; drop the nonnegative term M_n 1_{B_n} and write M_k = h + (M_k - h) on A_k. Sound. Second claim: the expected overshoot O_n = E0[sum_{k<=n}(M_k - h) 1_{A_k}] is nondecreasing in n because every summand is >= 0 (M_k >= h on A_k); it is positive from the first day n_0 with P(A_{n_0}) > 0 because M_{n_0} > h almost surely on A_{n_0} (shown in the previous sentence for the monitor); so P(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) <= (1 - O_n)/h = alpha (1 - O_n) <= alpha (1 - O_{n_0}) for n >= n_0, and letting n grow (monotone limit) the probability of ever crossing is at most alpha (1 - O_{n_0}) < alpha. Sound; for this monitor n_0 = 1 and the gap is tiny in absolute terms but strictly positive, and the sentence claims only 'strictly below alpha'. Numerical spot-check (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify8-L01-L02/overshoot.py, 40,000 null paths of the monitor with alpha = 0.05, kappa = 252, horizon 2520): P(cross) = 0.0199 < 0.05, E[overshoot] = 0.0191 > 0, h P + O = 0.417 <= E[W_n] = 0.989 <= 1. Notation: h, M_k, A_k, B_k and 'the same steps' refer to the proof of Theorem 6.4, which the sentence names; A_n of Proposition 6.1's proof is a different, proof-local event, so there is no collision inside either proof. I re-read the abstract (OpenAlex, curl 2026-10-19, no email, /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify9-L01-L02/dl/oa_10_2307_2530245.json): 'comparing two treatments when response to treatment is both dichotomous ... and immediate ... The maximum number (N) of tests and the number (m1 + m2) of observations collected between successive tests is fixed in advance. The overall size of the procedure is shown to be controlled with virtually the same accuracy as the single sample chi-square test ... The power is also found to be virtually the same.' That is a fixed-number-of-looks design, so a power finding about it supports a statement about 'a group-sequential design with a fixed number of looks', and 'can be cheap' is existential and says 'illustrates', not 'all such designs are'. (2) The second sentence moved to 'a spending design' (Lan and DeMets); its support is not the O'Brien-Fleming finding but the page's own argument two sentences later (nested events as in Proposition 6.1, positive probability by part (b), so a design that has spent all of alpha exceeds alpha once an uncovered look is added), which I re-derived (see L01-math-rem69-extralook). The Lan-DeMets abstract (OpenAlex, same date, dl/oa_10_1093_biomet_70_3_659.json) says the boundary 'is determined by alpha*(t), and by past and current decision times, but does not depend on the future decision times or the total number of decision times': a spending design is flexible about the number and timing of looks inside its budget and has no alpha left beyond it, which is what 'ends with its budget' says. (3) Consistency with the rest of the page, re-read: line 439 ('Pocock ... O'Brien and Fleming fix the maximum number of tests ... Lan and DeMets ... replace it with a function alpha*(t)'), quiz item 14's explanation ('Pocock and O'Brien-Fleming fix the number of looks in advance; Lan and DeMets free their number and timing but still spend a fixed alpha'), key-results row 13 and card S7-c146 all separate fixed-look designs from spending designs the same way. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'A false rejection' (lines 443-445)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-12 evidence: Re-derived. Almost surely every q_j > 0 (q_j = 0 only for one value of U), so the i - 1 zeros are p_(1) = ... = p_(i-1) = 0 and p_(i) = min_j q_j belongs to a true null. Zeros pass steps 1, ..., i - 1 because the constants are positive (the step fails only when p_(k) > c_k). If min_j q_j <= c <= c_i, step i passes, so the first failing index is > i and H_(i), a true null, is rejected. Hence FWER >= P(min q <= c) = m'c = min(m' c_i, 1) > alpha (m' c_i > alpha by hypothesis, 1 > alpha). The page states it as an inequality; the equality FWER = min(m' c_i, 1) also holds (step i is then decisive: it passes iff min q <= c_i, and the arcs of length c_i cover the circle when c_i >= 1/m'), which I confirmed numerically; the lesson does not need it. [git diff 202ea24..50d202e changes course/modules/S/S7/L02.html at line 88 only (the fwer-growth caption); the passage of this row is outside that line.]

unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-12 evidence: Re-derived and simulated. With c_i = alpha/m', c = alpha/m' (<= 1/m' because alpha < 1). If p_(i) = min q > alpha/m' step i fails with steps 1..i-1 passed, so only the i - 1 false nulls are rejected and V = 0; if min q <= alpha/m', H_(i) is rejected, V >= 1. Hence FWER = m' (alpha/m') = alpha, for every i = 1..m, i.e. m' = m..1 true nulls. The closing sentence ('Every inequality in the proof of Theorem 3.2 holds with equality here') checked line by line against Theorem 3.2's proof: j <= m - m_0 + 1 is an equality (j = i = m - m' + 1); alpha/(m + 1 - j) <= alpha/m_0 is an equality (m + 1 - j = m'); {V >= 1} contained in {min <= alpha/m_0} is an equality of events (just shown); Boole's inequality is an equality (disjoint events); validity is an equality (uniform). Numerical: for m = 1..8 and every i the exact-grid FWER of Holm under the construction is 0.05 to machine precision (max |FWER - 0.05| = 0). [git diff 202ea24..50d202e changes course/modules/S/S7/L02.html at line 88 only (the fwer-growth caption); the passage of this row is outside that line.]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'Zeros are a convenience' (line 448)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-12 evidence: Re-derived. False-null p-values in (0, delta] with delta <= c_j for all j < i: on {delta < min_j q_j <= c} the i - 1 smallest p-values are the false nulls' (each <= delta <= its constant, so steps 1..i-1 pass) and p_(i) = min q <= c <= c_i passes, so a true null is rejected. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'What it shows' (line 449)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-12 evidence: Checked sentence by sentence. (1) 'A step-down procedure with fixed constants that controls the FWER at level alpha under every joint distribution of valid p-values must have c_k <= alpha/(m + 1 - k) for every k': the contrapositive of the main result (positive constants, alpha < 1). (2) 'Raising constants only adds rejections, because the first failure moves later, so Holm's procedure rejects everything such a procedure rejects, for every vector of p-values': if c_k <= Holm_k for all k then p_(k) > Holm_k implies p_(k) > c_k, so the first failing index of the c-procedure is no later than Holm's and it rejects a subset. (3) 'A gain beyond Holm's needs the dependence between the tests (Lessons 4 and 5)': true for the class the problem treats (p-value step-down with fixed constants, every configuration of true nulls possible, only marginal validity). Outside that class gains can come from logical relations between the hypotheses (Shaffer 1986) as well as from dependence; the sentence is a pointer, sits after the sentence that fixes the class, and is not a graded claim span. Note, not a failure. (4) The T span after it matches Lehmann and Romano Theorem 2.3(ii) (L02-cite-lehmann2005generalizations). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Remark 3.5 (line 272), sentences 'Holm ... inherits Bonferroni's conservatism under positive correlation (Lab 1)' and 'Raising its constants would reduce that conservatism under positive correlation, but not safely'
rows.evidence: Re-checked at 0922fe8 (the line is unchanged since 584f614; the scope is re-derived). The sentences state a general effect of positive correlation, and the effect is not general. Positively correlated p-values can make Bonferroni's FWER equal alpha (row L02-cards-c018-dependence-clause). Holm is no better off: by Proposition 3.3 every Bonferroni rejection is a Holm rejection, so Holm's FWER is at least Bonferroni's, and by Theorem 3.2 it is at most alpha, so in that counterexample Holm's FWER is exactly alpha too. Lab 1 supports the effect only for equicorrelated Gaussian statistics, which is the lab's model. The Romano-Wolf claim span on the same line (B, data-cite romano2005stepwise, Abstract) is not affected and stays PASS in rows L02-cite-romano2005stepwise and L02-grade-romano.

Grade: BLUEPRINT section 3 gives B for one top-venue paper (Romano and Wolf, Econometrica 2005) whose claims are an asymptotic FWER theorem and a power comparison from the authors' simulation designs, with no independent replication found. B is right: not A (not replicated out of sample), not T (the control result is asymptotic and attributed, not proved on the page). Counter-evidence search (BLUEPRINT section 2, 'must cite its published counter-evidence if any exists'; VERIFIER_RULES 2.3). Method and counts are in row L02-cite-romano-counter-screen. Summary: (a) OpenAlex cites-filter for W3123939061 with no key and no mailto returned HTTP 429 until the daily reset and HTTP 200 after it (count 1013; pages 1 to 6 fetched by offset, because cursor paging requires a key, which was not requested). (b) OpenCitations index v2 (no key): 711 citing rows, 708 DOIs, 3 arXiv-only. (c) Crossref work records for the 708 DOIs (User-Agent only): 707 resolved, one DataCite dataset DOI returned 404; 298 Crossref abstracts; the RW record itself has is-referenced-by-count 770. (d) Key-set screen: 159 Crossref titles-or-abstracts and 178 OpenAlex titles-or-abstracts match the multiple-testing and power terms; 39 Crossref and 13 further OpenAlex abstracts name Romano/Wolf, step-down, stepwise, Holm, Bonferroni, FWER, single-step, StepM or reality check; 16 OpenAlex-only works also match. Result: no published work contests the page's claim. Stepwise-versus-stepwise comparisons only: Hsu, Hsu and Kuan (JEF 2010; SSRN abstract) and Hsu, Kuan and Yen (JFEC 2014; published abstract read in OpenAlex's journal record) say their stepwise SPA test is more powerful than Romano and Wolf's stepwise reality check 'under any power notion defined in Romano and Wolf (2005)'. Hansen (2005) compares SPA with White's single-step reality check. Corroboration, not contest: Clarke, Romano and Wolf (2020, Stata Journal; PDF read): the correction 'is considerably more powerful than earlier multiple-testing procedures, such as the Bonferroni and Holm corrections'; Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics (2023, doi 10.3389/fams.2023.1151314; full text read): 'in all scenarios we considered, Romano and Wolf's method uniformly outperformed methods other than the one we propose' (Bonferroni, Holm, minP and Westfall-Young step-down among them); Romano and Wolf (2007, Annals of Statistics, doi 10.1214/009053606000001622; cited by 123 in the screened set) concerns generalized error rates (k-FWER), not the power comparison. Not read in full, stated plainly: Harvey and Liu's evaluation of alternative multiple-testing methods for finance (RAPS 2020, doi 10.1093/rapstu/raaa003) has an abstract that states no finding ('we provide simulation evidence on the relative performance of different methods'), and its full text is behind an OUP Cloudflare challenge (HTTP 403); the Econometrica publisher page is HTTP 403 (its Econometric Society page was read in round 11); the JFEC 2014 publisher page is HTTP 403 (its journal-record abstract was read via OpenAlex); the JEF 2010 publisher page is a captcha (its SSRN abstract was read). The B span names no counter-evidence and none was found that contests it, so the row passes. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/cards.json S7-c187 (lesson L02, grade T); course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Proposition 3.3 (lines 196-204)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-12 evidence: Re-checked from scratch. Proposition 3.3 (L02.html 196-204): 'For any p-values, every hypothesis rejected by the Bonferroni correction at level α is rejected by Holm's procedure at level α.' Its proof: 'Suppose Bonferroni rejects H_(b), so p_(b) ≤ α/m. For every b' ≤ b, p_(b') ≤ p_(b) ≤ α/m ≤ α/(m+1−b'), because m+1−b' ≤ m. So Holm passes steps 1..b, and its first failure, if any, comes after b. Hence Holm rejects H_(b).' Card back: 'Yes (Proposition 3.3). If Bonferroni rejects H_(b), then p_(b) ≤ α/m, and for every b' ≤ b, p_(b') ≤ p_(b) ≤ α/m ≤ α/(m + 1 − b'), so Holm passes steps 1 to b and rejects H_(b).' The card is the proof's core step and the statement's conclusion, one fact, correct, grade T (proved on the page, no cite needed; cf. S7-c002). Numerical check (scratch scripts/card_numbers.py, python -I, numpy): 48,000 random p-vectors for m = 1..12 with mixed small and large p-values at α = 0.05: 71,294 Bonferroni rejections, and 0 cases in which Bonferroni rejects a hypothesis Holm does not. Card id S7-c187 is unique and the schema passes.

unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-12 evidence: New sentence: 'testing each hypothesis at α/m holds the family-wise error rate at or below α for every m, and here, with independent nulls, at exactly α only when m = 1.' Derivation: by Boole's inequality (as in the proof of Theorem 2.2), the FWER of m true nulls each tested at α/m is at most m·(α/m) = α for any dependence, so 'at or below α for every m' holds. With independent true nulls, FWER = 1 − (1 − α/m)^m. Bernoulli's inequality (1 − x)^m ≥ 1 − mx holds with strict inequality for m ≥ 2 and 0 < x < 1, so FWER < α for m ≥ 2; at m = 1 the FWER is exactly α. Numerical check (scratch scripts/card_numbers.py, python -I, .venv): for α = 0.01..0.10 and m = 1..200, 500, 1000, 5000: 0 violations of FWER ≤ α; strictly below α for every m ≥ 2; |FWER − α| ≤ 1e-15 at m = 1. Values: α = 0.05: FWER(2) = 0.049375, FWER(1000) = 0.048772; α = 0.01: FWER(1000) = 0.009950. The figure's readout and desc in every state agree (row L02-fig-fwer-growth).

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Remark 3.5 claim span (line 272, data-cite romano2005stepwise) and key-results row 8 (line 530); the counter-evidence search for the grade B
rows.evidence: unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-12 evidence: Method (round 12, 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-20). Question: does any published work contest the claim that the Romano-Wolf stepwise bootstrap controls the FWER asymptotically with more power than single-step methods (L02 Remark 3.5 and key-results row 8)? Sources, each fetched this round with a User-Agent header only (no e-mail, no mailto, no key). (1) OpenCitations index v2, https://api.opencitations.net/index/v2/citations/doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2005.00615.x: 711 citing rows; 708 distinct citing DOIs; 3 rows are arXiv IDs only (1812.04345, 2103.09603, 2107.10017). (2) Crossref work records for the 708 DOIs: 707 resolved; 1 DataCite dataset DOI (10.4225/03/5935ff87c8d5c) returned 404; 298 carry an abstract. The RW record has is-referenced-by-count 770, so about 60 Crossref-counted citers are outside OpenCitations; Crossref has no citers filter (reference.doi and reference-doi are rejected with HTTP 400), so those were not screened. (3) OpenAlex cites filter for W3123939061: HTTP 429 until the daily reset at 00:00 UTC, then HTTP 200 with count 1013 (pages 1 to 6 by offset; cursor paging needs a key, which was not requested): 972 with a DOI (968 distinct), of which 658 are in the OpenCitations set and 310 are OpenAlex-only; 607 carry an abstract. (4) Screens: title or abstract matches the key set (multiple testing, power, Romano, Wolf, step-down, stepwise, Holm, Bonferroni, FWER, single-step, StepM, reality check): 159 of 707 Crossref records and 178 of 1013 OpenAlex works. Contest set (Romano, Wolf, step-down, stepwise, Holm, Bonferroni, family-wise, FWER, single-step, StepM, reality check) in title or abstract: 39 Crossref records; 13 further OpenCitations records through OpenAlex abstracts (for 151 of the 409 records without a Crossref abstract); 16 OpenAlex-only works. (5) Contest-set records without a Crossref abstract were checked against OpenAlex (13 of them have one, read in (4)). The rest were screened by title and venue: applications (Empirical Economics 2015; Decision Support Systems 2010); method papers whose titles make no power claim about Romano-Wolf (Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference 2014; Statistics and Probability Letters 2016 twice; SSRN 2016); and the JFEC 2014 record, whose publisher abstract is read in (6) from OpenAlex. 258 of the 409 records without a Crossref abstract have no abstract in either source and were screened by title only. (6) Abstracts and texts read, with verdicts. Hansen (2005, SSRN 264569; JBES 2005): the SPA test is more powerful than White's single-step Reality Check; not about Romano-Wolf; no contest. Hsu, Hsu and Kuan (SSRN 1087044; JEF 2010, doi 10.1016/j.jempfin.2010.01.001): the stepwise SPA test 'is more powerful than the stepwise Reality Check test of Romano and Wolf (2005)'; a stepwise-versus-stepwise comparison; no contest (the JEF page returned a captcha, so the SSRN abstract was read). Hsu, Kuan and Yen (JFEC 2014, doi 10.1093/jjfinec/nbu014; abstract from the OpenAlex journal record): Step-SPA(k) is 'more powerful than Step-RC(k) under any power notion defined in Romano and Wolf (2005)'; no single-step comparison; no contest (the Oxford University Press page is a Cloudflare challenge, HTTP 403). Market-timing rule performance (JFEC 2011, doi 10.1093/jjfinec/nbq032): applies the RC, SPA and stepwise tests; no RW-versus-single-step comparison; no contest. Survey expectations and adjustments for multiple testing (JEBO 2024): 'The Bonferroni correction and related approaches ... are conservative and result in low power when the null hypotheses are false'; supports the page's comparison; not a contest. Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics (2023, doi 10.3389/fams.2023.1151314; full text read): 'in all scenarios we considered, Romano and Wolf's method uniformly outperformed methods other than the one we propose' (Bonferroni, Holm, minP and Westfall-Young step-down among them); corroborates. Clarke, Romano and Wolf (2020, Stata Journal, doi 10.1177/1536867x20976314; PDF read): the correction is 'considerably more powerful than earlier multiple-testing procedures, such as the Bonferroni and Holm corrections'; corroborates. arXiv 2107.10017 (2021 preprint on cluster-randomised trials; abstract read): 'the Romano-Wolf type procedure ... is more efficient than the other methods in a simulation-based study'; corroborates (preprint). Harvey and Liu, 'False (and Missed) Discoveries in Financial Economics' (arXiv 2006.04269, 2020; abstract read): 'Evaluating current methods, we find that they lack power to detect outperforming managers'; a general claim about current methods with no RW-versus-single-step comparison in the abstract; not a contest as scoped; the Journal of Finance full text was not read. Harvey and Liu's evaluation for finance (RAPS 2020, doi 10.1093/rapstu/raaa003): the abstract states no finding; the full text is behind an OUP challenge (HTTP 403); not read. Extended MinP tests (arXiv 1911.04696; Econometric Reviews 2026): combination tests; no RW power claim. Testing many moment inequalities (WP 2013): Bonferroni and multiplier-bootstrap critical values; no RW comparison in the abstract. The Stepwise Cauchy Combination Test (JFEC 2025, doi 10.1093/jjfinec/nbaf020; Crossref abstract): 'more powerful than conventional multiple testing corrections'; a newer competitor, not a contest of Romano-Wolf against single-step methods (freshness flag). (7) Result: no contest found in any screened source. Limits, stated plainly: about 60 Crossref-counted citers are not in the OpenCitations list and were not screened; 258 records have no abstract; the RAPS 2020 full text and the Econometrica, JFEC 2014 and JEF 2010 publisher pages were not readable (HTTP 403 or captcha). These limits are recorded in the registry flags.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Theorem 2.2 (lines 98-110); cards.json S7-c018 back, clause (a)
rows.evidence: Clause (a): 'Theorem 2.2 still holds it at or below α under any dependence'. L02.html lines 98-103 state Theorem 2.2 (T): 'If every true-null p-value is valid, then for any joint distribution of (p_1, ..., p_m) the Bonferroni correction satisfies FWER <= (m_0/m) alpha <= alpha.' The proof (lines 107-109) uses only Boole's inequality and validity: 'Boole's inequality holds for any events whatever their dependence, so no assumption about the joint distribution entered.' The card's words match the theorem, and T is the right grade because the theorem is proved on the page. The same statement is key-results row 2 of L02 (T, 'Proved in §2', line 524). Spot check: the proof's bound m_0 alpha/m <= alpha for m_0 <= m is immediate; the card needs no other number.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P1 (lines 408-415; solution line 412); cards.json S7-c018 back, clause (b)
rows.evidence: Clause (b). P1 (L02.html lines 408-415): 'Suppose all m hypotheses are true and all m p-values are equal to one uniform random variable U.' Solution (line 412): 'With equal p-values, Bonferroni rejects all or none, so its FWER is Prob(U <= alpha/m) = alpha/m.' Re-derived: the m rejection events {p_i <= alpha/m} all equal {U <= alpha/m}, a single event of probability alpha/m for uniform U. Numerical spot check (scratch c018_check.py, numpy default_rng(13013), 4,000,000 draws): Bonferroni FWER = 0.000974 against alpha/m = 0.001000 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.000016). The card's 'the m identical rejection events form one event' matches the page's 'the union of m_0 identical events is one event' (line 129). T is right.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/cards.json S7-c018 back, clause (c) 'but positive dependence wastes part of that budget'; the same claim in the lesson text at L02.html line 129 (row L02-claim-line129)
rows.evidence: Clause (c) is graded T. BLUEPRINT section 3 gives T only to results proved on the page. The page proves the extreme case (P1, all p-values equal) and nothing about general positive dependence. The general claim is also false as stated. Counterexample, re-derived and computed in scratch (c018_check.py; numpy default_rng(13013)): let U be uniform on [0,1), c = alpha/m = 0.001, m = 50 tests, all null, p_i = (U + (i-1)c) mod 1. Each p_i is uniform, so every null is valid and Theorem 2.2 applies. The rejection events {p_i <= c} are 50 consecutive arcs of length c that tile an arc of length 50c = 0.05, so they are pairwise disjoint and P(union) = 0.05 = alpha = (m_0/m) alpha. Monte Carlo: FWER = 0.050006 over 4,000,000 draws, and never more than one rejection in a draw. The pairwise Pearson correlations of the p-values are 1 - 6d(1-d) with d = |i-j|c, which lies in [0.7204, 0.9940] (exact, 1225 pairs); the Monte Carlo minimum is 0.7189 and the maximum 0.9948. So every pair is positively correlated and the bound is attained. Two-null version: Monte Carlo FWER 0.001963 against 2c = 0.002, correlation 0.9941. Therefore 'positive dependence wastes part of that budget' is not a theorem, and the page's own Problem P2 (line 416) already shows the bound is attained when the rejection events are disjoint. What the page can prove is that the bound is loose when the rejection events overlap (P1 is the extreme of overlap). The literature restricts the positive-correlation effect to the equicorrelated normal setup: Das and Bhandari (SPL 168, 2021, doi 10.1016/j.spl.2020.108943) and Dey and Bhandari (SPL 193, 2023, doi 10.1016/j.spl.2022.109700), read as arXiv abstracts in row L02-cards-c221-grade. The effect is supported by Lab 1 only, at grade C (S7-c221).
rows.fix: Remove clause (c) from the S7-c018 back: this is part of the fix in row L02-cards-c018-grade. Do not restate the claim as T on any card. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/cards.json S7-c221 grade 'C', basis 'Lab 1 (simulation)'; counter-evidence search for the claim (VERIFIER_RULES 2.3)
rows.evidence: Grade rule: a result established by a seeded simulation lab is grade C with that lab as basis (BUILDER_RULES 7; the brief). Lab 1 is seeded (np.random.default_rng(2002)) and its code is labelled '# SIMULATED global null' (line 138), so C with basis 'Lab 1 (simulation)' is the right grade and basis form. Lesson consistency: the front (50 one-sided tests, all nulls true, alpha = 5%, pairwise correlation rho) is Lab 1's setup exactly. Counter-evidence search: (1) Crossref query.bibliographic 'Bonferroni correction dependence conservative family-wise error rate correlated tests' (44,303 results; top 8 read); (2) Crossref query.bibliographic 'Bonferroni test positively correlated test statistics FWER below nominal level' (772,761 results; top 8 read, generic reference entries). Two relevant SPL titles: Das and Bhandari, 'Bound on FWER for correlated normal', Statistics and Probability Letters 168 (2021) 108943, doi 10.1016/j.spl.2020.108943; and Dey and Bhandari, 'FWER goes to zero for correlated normal', SPL 193 (2023) 109700, doi 10.1016/j.spl.2022.109700. Crossref and OpenAlex carry no abstract for either; ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403. The arXiv API (export.arxiv.org, 2026-10-20) gave their preprint abstracts. Das and Bhandari (arXiv 2019-08-06): for equicorrelated normal statistics, 'an upper bound on the FWER of Bonferroni-alpha procedure is alpha(1-rho)', and 'Bonferroni's method actually controls the FWER at a much smaller level ... under the positively correlated case'. Dey and Bhandari (arXiv 2021-10-11): 'in the equicorrelated normal setup with positive equicorrelation, Bonferroni FWER tends to zero asymptotically'. Both support Lab 1's direction and both restrict it to equicorrelated normal statistics, so neither contests S7-c221 (their published versions were not read). No contest found, so PASS. The two titles are registry flags. Search depth limit: two Crossref queries, two arXiv records.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 129 (the paragraph after Example 2.4): 'The bound in (1) becomes loose when tests are positively dependent. In the extreme where all null p-values are equal, ... The next lab measures what happens in between.'
rows.evidence: The first sentence is an ungraded substantive claim (no claim span, no citation key; BLUEPRINT section 3), and it is false as a general statement. The counterexample in row L02-cards-c018-dependence-clause gives 50 valid, pairwise positively correlated p-values (correlations 0.72 to 0.99) with FWER exactly alpha = (m_0/m) alpha, so the bound is not loose there. The page's own Problem P2 (lines 416-423) shows the bound attained for disjoint rejection events. The defensible statements are: the bound is loose when the rejection events overlap (the extreme of P1), and it is attained when they are disjoint (P2). The sentence about the next lab is accurate once the lab is named as equicorrelated Gaussian (Lab 1, grade C). The extreme-case sentence (P1, T) is correct as written.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html quiz item 8 (prompt line 596: 'As the correlation between test statistics rises, Bonferroni's actual FWER...'; keyed option 'falls below α, towards α/m'; explanation line 602)
rows.evidence: The prompt is general, and the keyed answer is right only in the scope of Lab 1. The explanation 'Lab 1 and Problem P1' is right for the scoped prompt. Other quiz items on dependence are correct as keyed: 'Which assumption does Theorem 2.2 need?' (answer: none, only valid true-null p-values) and 'Can Holm's procedure reject fewer hypotheses than Bonferroni?' (answer: no, never, Proposition 3.3).

rows.evidence: BLUEPRINT section 3: every substantive claim carries an evidence grade and a citation key, and grade D must be marked 'It is widely claimed...'. Three empirical generalisations about correlation carry neither. (i) L02 line 347: 'Lab 1 shows Bonferroni's actual FWER at a tenth of its nominal level when tests are highly correlated, which is the usual case for variants of one strategy.' The first clause is Lab 1's result (0.0056 / 0.05 = 0.112, row L02-cards-c221-numbers); 'the usual case for variants of one strategy' is an unsourced empirical claim. (ii) L01 line 79: 'the Z_n are typically correlated, in a pattern the researcher rarely knows'. (iii) L01 line 448: 'real variants (a 50-day versus a 55-day lookback) are highly correlated'. None is a lab result, none is in the registry, and none is marked D. The shared-history sentence is an explanation and needs no change beyond the modal wording. The overlap of a 50-day and a 55-day lookback ending on one day is arithmetic (50 of 55 days), so it can be stated on the page without a grade.

A 2025 stepwise competitor exists: 'A Stepwise Cauchy Combination Test for Multiple Testing Problems with Financial Applications' (Journal of Financial Econometrics 2025, doi 10.1093/jjfinec/nbaf020, read in round 12 from Crossref), whose abstract says it is 'more powerful than conventional multiple testing corrections' and keeps strong familywise error control under dependence. Not in the registry and not cited. L02 Remark 3.5 and key-results row 8 concern the 2005 procedure only, so it is not a defect; a debate-brief revision of the stepwise material should mention it and compare it with Romano-Wolf directly.

Recent applications in the OpenAlex set (2024 to 2026) use the Romano-Wolf correction; one (a Thai REIT diversification study, Journal of Risk and Financial Management 2026) reports that Romano-Wolf finds a significant improvement where Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg find none. These are applications, not tests of the power claim; another (School Breaks and Crime, Journal of Quantitative Criminology 2026) only applies Romano-Wolf step-down p-values.

Published corroboration read in round 12: Clarke, Romano and Wolf (2020, Stata Journal) and the 2023 Frontiers simulation study (doi 10.3389/fams.2023.1151314) both report the Romano-Wolf method as more powerful than Bonferroni and Holm in their settings. A debate brief on stepwise methods should cite them alongside Hsu, Kuan and Yen (2014, JFEC), which shows that a stepwise SPA variant beats the Romano-Wolf stepwise reality check.
